claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Certain alloying-element additions induce phase transformations in the high-entropy alloy.
Certain alloying-element additions promote segregation in the high-entropy alloy.
The added alloying elements lower the thermodynamic barrier for phase transformation.
Lowering the phase-transformation barrier causes the added elements to segregate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation of the added elements causes brittle intermetallic phases to nucleate and grow.
The resulting intermetallic phases are localized along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary intermetallic phases act as crack-initiation sites.
Crack initiation at brittle intermetallic phases reduces the alloy's toughness under mechanical loading.
The alloying additions can lead to brittle fracture under demanding mechanical loads.
Specimens containing the alloying additions will have lower fracture toughness than the untreated single-phase baseline.
Specimens containing the alloying additions will have lower impact energy than the untreated single-phase baseline.
Microscopy of specimens containing the alloying additions will reveal brittle intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries that are absent from the untreated baseline.
High strain rates, low temperatures, or corrosive conditions accelerate phase-transformation kinetics and phase segregation.
The proposed behavior applies under demanding service conditions involving high strain rate, low temperature, or corrosive exposure.
An otherwise identically processed alloy without the additions provides the control for isolating the effect of the alloying intervention.
